thread.title: Door hinge pins
thread.first_post_html: Going to replace the pins and bushings in my door hinges. Any tips on how to do it. I guess you need two people, one to hold door up while the other bangs out old pin and installs new?

posts.post_content_html: Going to replace the pins and bushings in my door hinges. Any tips on how to do it. I guess you need two people, one to hold door up while the other bangs out old pin and installs new?
If you use a floor jack to hold up the door, it's alot easier with 2 people. I do it at work by myself using a engine lift.

make sure you got the prop tool for the door spring as pryin with a screw driver or any such as that is not safe. Get the right tool for spring and its pretty pancake remember the bushings in the hinges are different sizes. do one pin at a time

Originally Posted by Anthoney456
make sure you got the prop tool for the door spring as pryin with a screw driver or any such as that is not safe.

You could also compress the spring in a vise and use wire to keep it compressed. When you get it in un-twist the wire and it will pop in place.

yeah, I gotta do this too... a floor jack, or cherry picker sounds like the right tool to support the door.

http://www.hotrodautosupply.com/esho...d&productId=12

x11teen on the door spring tool. I bought mine for around $15 and it was worth every penny.

I used a floor jack and a block of wood under the door and I tied the top to a lift arm to keep it from tipping.

Yeah, I'm not fond of the vise for the spring. I know a lot of guys have done it this way but one try sent it flying for me and I considered myself lucky it didn't fly into my face. The correct tool for the job is CHEAP. A lot cheaper than a visit to the hospital to sew up where your eye used to be.

I do the engine hoist method too. Just be sure you protect the door frame and window channel. I wrap a thick towel around the frame and then use a strap around that, hung from the hoist. One man job this way.



You can see the full range of these pics at: www.someotherplace.com/guides/hinges01.jpg through hinges23.jpg, just keep changing the numbers to see the progress. It was a quick-n-dirty pictorial so just remember, the advice is worth what you paid for it.

BTW if your truck is close to the right height, you can prop something under the door like a milk crate instead, and still one-man it. It's just tricky to manuever the door around without scratching it or the fender.

One FINAL NOTE that is important. If you've got power windows, DO NOT, DO NOT, DO NOT close the door while the harnesses are disconnected. If the connectors are just hanging out in the door jamb, you will almost surely bust the crap out of them when the door closes!

*Added 9/22/10 - if you want to see what letting them get really bad does, check out: www.someotherplace.com/guides/hinges25.jpg, www.someotherplace.com/guides/hinges26.jpg, www.someotherplace.com/guides/hinges27.jpg ! NASTY...

*Added 9/22/10 - if you let the sagging door condition go too long, it will "egg out" the hole in the top hinge half on the door side. This means once you do bushings and pins, it will still sag and have slop, and wear out too soon. The only "official" fix for this is to replace the hinge, which is a MAJOR pain, and the hinges are expensive. A hack fix which actually works long-term is to go ahead and replace everything, but ditch the upper retainer for that top pin. Scrape away the paint from the hinge area immediately surrounding the pin and also an area lower on the same hinge to attach the welder ground to. Jack the door up with a block of wood from the rear so it pushes the slack in the hole forwards toward the front of the truck. Stitch just a LITTLE BIT of weld to fill up the hole and retain the pin. Don't put too much because if you ever need to remove the door later (like to replace from a crash) you have very little room to work to cut the weld for removing the pin. THIS FIX WORKS.

Richard

I just installed oversized busings and they seem to fit like a champ. I also put another door on my truck b/c I had some damage on the other. Now my truck is still hitting and I found the problem.
Its the very top hole on the top hinge that is connected to the door itself. It seems this whole is a little egged out. bc you can lift the door up and down slightly and see it moving. I know on this hinge the pin goes up from the bottom. I guess Im gonna have to replace the hinge thats welded to the door? The store said they sold me oversize bushings but there was no such thing as oversized door pins.

Roll back up and look at post #8 in regards to the egged-out hole in the hinge.

But also, sometimes pulling a door from another truck is a big problem. If you got it from a considerably newer model, they can often not fit no matter how hard you try. I've had people debate this with me but I've got a ton of experience in that area; you are best off getting a door from a truck that is very close in year model to yours.

Richard

I recently replaced the door hinge pins in my driver door on my 94 G van. I used a floor jack but there wasn't enough room to work on the hinge so I had to remove the hinge from the van. I marked both sides of the hinge on the body and door so I knew where it had to go to get it to line up. Worked perfect! made it a lot easier to replace the bushings too.

post_rewrites.rewritten_content: Replacing the pins and bushings in your door hinges requires careful handling. It's recommended to have two people: one to hold the door steady while the other removes the old pin and installs the new one.
Using a floor jack to raise a vehicle is generally easier with two people. At work, I accomplish this task alone with an engine lift.

Ensure you have the proper tool for the door spring, such as a prop tool, as using a screwdriver can be unsafe. Use the correct tool designed for springs, which are typically flat like a pancake. Remember that bushings in the hinges come in different sizes. Remove one pin at a time.

Make sure to use the proper pry tool for removing the door spring, as prying with a screwdriver can be unsafe. Alternatively, compress the spring in a vise and hold it with wire. Once removed, untwist the wire to allow the spring to snap into place.

I need to use a floor jack or a cherry picker to properly support the door. You can find them at [Hot Rod Auto Supply](http://www.hotrodautosupply.com/eshop/productDetails.jsp?categoryId=50649&productId=12).

x11teen recommends using a door spring tool, which they purchased for approximately $15 and found to be well worth the cost. For the job, they used a floor jack, placed a block of wood under the door, and secured the top to a lift arm to prevent tipping.

I prefer using an engine hoist method for installing hinges, as it is safer and more efficient. A thick towel wrapped around the door frame with a strap secured by the hoist works well. This is a one-man job. For detailed step-by-step images, see www.someotherplace.com/guides/hinges01.jpg through hinges23.jpg.

For those with slightly lower trucks, propping the door open with a milk crate can simplify the process, but be cautious to avoid scratches.

If you have power windows, do not close the door while disconnecting harnesses. This could damage the window connectors.

An important note: Excessive sagging can "egg out" the top hinge hole, leading to premature wear and potential issues even after bushings and pins are installed. In such cases, replacing the entire hinge is necessary but difficult. A practical workaround is to remove the upper retainer, clean the hinge area, and perform a spot weld to fill the hole without restricting future removal of the door.

This fix ensures long-term reliability.

Does anyone have the part number for replacement pins? Please provide the year of your truck. Note that if there's significant play, you might need an oversized bushing. Installation is straightforward.

My 90 k1500 had been sagging due to worn out bushings on the bottom hinge before I purchased it. After installing oversized bushings, the fit seemed good, but the truck still hit. The issue turned out to be a slightly deformed top hole in the top hinge connected to the door. Since the pin moves up from the bottom on this hinge, it appears that replacing the welded hinge is necessary. Unfortunately, the store did not have oversized door pins available.

Review post #8 regarding the hinge issue. When replacing a door, consider that using one from a significantly newer model can lead to compatibility problems despite your efforts. For optimal results, obtain a door from a truck with a similar year model to yours. I have extensive experience supporting this advice.
